blocks.text: Forsskål, in Descript. Animall. p. 15, mentions a certain serpent which he calls Coluber Baetaen, whose Arabic name he writes بتن [btn]. This, however, rendered according to the popular pronunciation, I think is miswritten for فتن [ftn], which is our very פתן. Forsskål describes this serpent in these words: Spotted all over with white and black. Length a foot; thickness almost two inches. Oviparous. Its bite kills instantly, the wounded body swelling up. The opinion of Oedmann (Vermischte Sammlung. fasc. 5, ch. 10, p. 85) seems to me hardly probable, that this snake is not different from the Coluber Lebetinus Linn., which is frequent on the island of Cyprus, where it bears the name ἀσπιδος [aspidos]. Forsskål (p. 13) says the length of its body is under a cubit, Hasselquist (p. 239) one foot. Both, however, agree that its bite brings on a lethal sleep. The common people on the island of Cyprus consider this serpent deaf, and hence it is also called κουφη [kouphē], deaf (see Pococke, Itinerar. vol. 2, § 402, and Forsskål, Descript. Animall. p. 14). And since in Ps. LVIII, 5. the פתן is called deaf, Michaelis in Supplemm. vol. 6, p. 2056, and Oedmann loc. cit. p. 84 think that the פתן of the Hebrews is the same serpent as the Coluber Lebetinus Linn. But since more than one kind of serpent is believed to be deaf, as Bochart shows in the following Chapter, and the Coluber Lebetinus seems to be native only to Cyprus, I think it more certain to take Forsskål's Coluber Baetaen for the פתן of the Hebrews.
